An autocracy is a system of government in which one single person holds complete and unlimited power over an entire country. That one person — called an autocrat — makes all the important decisions alone, without needing anyone's approval, and nobody has the legal or political authority to stop them, overrule them, or hold them accountable.

Think of it this way: in most modern governments, power is shared and controlled. Laws limit what leaders can do. Courts can say "no, that's illegal." Citizens can vote leaders out. In an autocracy, none of that applies to the ruler. They are, essentially, above everything and everyone.
What Makes a Government an Autocracy?

There are three defining features that, together, make a government an autocracy:

1. Power concentrated in one person.
All major decisions — about war, law, economy, and citizens' lives — flow from a single individual. There is no meaningful co-ruler, no cabinet that can override them, and no legislative body with real authority.

2. No accountability.
The ruler does not answer to the people, to a constitution, or to any institution. They cannot be legally removed from power through elections, impeachment, or votes of no confidence. If accountability exists at all, it exists only on paper, not in practice.

3. No effective checks and balances.
In healthy governments, different branches (executive, legislative, judicial) watch over each other to prevent any one branch from becoming too powerful. In an autocracy, those checks either don't exist or have been made meaningless. Courts, parliaments, and laws serve the ruler, not the other way around.
How Does an Autocrat Stay in Power?

An autocracy doesn't simply declare itself and then run smoothly. Autocrats use a combination of tools to maintain their grip:

  • Force and fear — Police, the military, and intelligence agencies are used to suppress opposition. People who speak out risk imprisonment, violence, or worse.
  • Propaganda — State-controlled media shapes what citizens hear, read, and believe, often portraying the ruler as heroic, necessary, or divinely chosen.
  • Elimination of rivals — Political opponents, independent journalists, and powerful institutions are weakened, co-opted, or destroyed.
  • Loyalty networks — The ruler rewards loyal supporters (military generals, business elites, party members) with wealth and privilege, giving them a personal reason to keep the autocrat in power.

Autocracy is a broad category. It contains several specific forms:

  • Absolute monarchy — The ruler is a king or queen (or emperor) who inherited their position and faces no legal limits on their power. The historical Tsars of Russia and many ancient pharaohs of Egypt are examples.
  • Dictatorship — The ruler typically came to power through force (a military coup, for example) rather than inheritance. Adolf Hitler's Germany and Joseph Stalin's Soviet Union are defining examples.
  • One-party state — Technically, a party is in charge, but in practice, the top individual within that party holds all real power. North Korea under the Kim family is a modern example.

What all of these share is the same root: one person, unchecked power.
Autocracy vs. Similar Words (and How They Differ)

These words are closely related to autocracy but are not identical:

  • Democracy — The direct opposite. Power belongs to the people, exercised through free elections, free speech, and independent courts.
  • Oligarchy — Rule by a small group of people (wealthy elites, a military council, etc.), not just one person. An oligarchy is not an autocracy unless one person within the group eventually dominates everyone else.
  • Totalitarianism — A more extreme form of autocracy. Not only does the ruler control the government, but they attempt to control all aspects of life — culture, religion, family, thought, and expression. All totalitarian states are autocracies, but not all autocracies are fully totalitarian.
  • Authoritarianism — A broader term for any system where political freedom is severely restricted and the ruler governs without meaningful consent. Autocracy is a specific, extreme kind of authoritarianism — the kind where one individual holds all the power.
  • Tyranny — Historically, this referred to a ruler who seized power illegitimately and governed cruelly. Today, it's often used interchangeably with autocracy but carries a stronger moral judgment — it emphasizes the abuse of power, not just the structure of it.
How the Word Is Used in Practice

In its strictest sense, "autocracy" is a political science term used to describe a form of government. For example:

"Russia under the Tsars was a classic autocracy — the emperor's word was law, and no institution could legally challenge him."

"The country descended into autocracy after the military coup dissolved the parliament and suspended the constitution."

However, you will also encounter the word used more loosely in everyday language to describe any person — not just a national leader — who exercises excessive, unchecked control over others:

"He ran the company like an autocracy — every decision went through him, and no one else's opinion mattered."

This looser use is common and understood, but when used in political or academic writing, autocracy specifically refers to governmental systems.

Knowing the word family helps you recognize this concept in different forms:

  • Autocracy (noun) — the system itself ("living under an autocracy")
  • Autocrat (noun) — the person who rules ("the autocrat signed the decree")
  • Autocratic (adjective) — describing the style of rule ("an autocratic leader," "autocratic tendencies")
  • Autocratically (adverb) — describing how something is done ("the country was governed autocratically")
If you ever need to recall this word quickly: an autocracy is a government where one person rules with total, unchecked power, answerable to no one.
